claims.text: Moderate thermal exposure causes the non-equilibrium supersaturated solid solution to decompose by diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth.
Decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution produces discrete intermetallic precipitates.
The intermetallic precipitates form at grain boundaries and within grains.
Mg-rich or other element-rich intermetallic phases are plausible products in Mg-containing lightweight alloys.
Intermetallic precipitation modifies the local chemical environment of the matrix and grain boundaries.
Intermetallic phases may preferentially oxidize and thereby promote or stabilize a protective oxide barrier.
A protective oxide-rich surface film can enhance passivation and reduce corrosion current density in an Mg-containing alloy.
Intermetallic/matrix interfaces may create galvanic couples that accelerate corrosion.
The initial mechanically alloyed and spark-plasma-sintered material is a metastable, single-phase, supersaturated solid solution.
The fraction of intermetallic precipitates will increase with annealing duration at 450 °C.
The size of intermetallic precipitates will increase with annealing duration at 450 °C.
The extent of intermetallic evolution will correlate with measurable changes in corrosion resistance.
The extent of intermetallic evolution will correlate with measurable changes in high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Intermetallic-assisted formation or stabilization of a protective oxide film would improve corrosion or oxidation resistance.
Galvanic coupling introduced by intermetallic precipitates would deteriorate corrosion resistance.
The initial homogeneous solid-solution state has high corrosion resistance because of its homogeneity.
The initial homogeneous solid-solution state has high-temperature oxidation resistance because of its homogeneity.
Annealing at about 450 °C for up to 100 hours is sufficient for noticeable diffusion and intermetallic nucleation.
Annealing at about 450 °C for up to 100 hours will not bring the alloy to full equilibrium.
